extracted.intended_audience: ACM CHI paper reviewers / SIGCHI peer reviewers (CHI 2022 reviewers)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting fair, equitable, and constructive peer reviews of CHI conference submissions, emphasizing contribution-focused evaluation, methodological transparency, accessibility, and awareness of cultural/positional biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair and equitable reviewing responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing, it is your responsibility to our community to provide a fair and equitable review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should center fairness and equity as a primary obligation when evaluating submissions; this is the overarching standard that informs all detailed guidance below.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility of the publication and materials
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the paper, figures, tables, supplementary materials, videos, previews, and other content are accessible. Let authors know in your review if they should make their materials more accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on contributions over form
rubrics_metrics.description: Contributions, contributions, contributions! Don’t get caught up in form over function: focus on the core of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the substantive contributions (including replication) rather than letting presentation, format, or stylistic issues dominate your judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-penalize non-native English / minor writing style issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Many authors are writing a CHI paper in a second or third language, which is a huge feat and has no bearing on the HCI work that has been done, which should be the focus of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English grammar and writing style points are minor review points. Ask: Is the writing able to communicate the main ideas? Can the authors benefit from a revision cycle for writing issues you identified? Prefer suggesting revisions rather than rejection for language problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the writing able to communicate the main ideas?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the manuscript conveys its main ideas clearly. If unclear, specify whether issues are remediable by revision and give actionable suggestions to help authors communicate their contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid imposing Western academic style preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Are your writing critiques based on preferences of Western academic standards (e.g. the Oxford comma, grammar minimalism, parallel writing structure)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious that stylistic preferences tied to Western academic norms should not be conflated with substantive flaws. Distinguish preference from actual barriers to understanding or scholarly rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope and claims of generalizability
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper only apply to populations in the author’s country? If so, suggest the authors specify their scope, rather than implying that what they found in their region is generalizable to the whole world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If findings are geographically, culturally, or demographically specific, ask authors to clearly state scope and limits of generalizability instead of assuming global applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of sample specificity and privilege differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the group studied specialized? Is there a difference of privilege within the scope of the population surveyed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the sampled population is specialized and whether intra-group privilege or heterogeneity affects interpretation. Ask authors to clarify sampling choices and implications for interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of methodology
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for transparency rather than debating the value of the methodology. Verify that authors are clear and precise in presenting their approach(es). Do not 'block' a contribution solely because of epistemological differences; instead assess whether the methodology is described transparently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological clarity and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the methodology clear? Could you replicate the study based on what was communicated?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the methods are specified with sufficient detail for replication or reasonable reuse. Point out missing details that prevent reproducibility and request clarifications or additional information where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare and limit your expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Be honest about your expertise! If a paper uses a methodology outside of your everyday experiences or expertise, then acknowledge what you do or do not know: both authors and reviewers have positionality!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State explicitly in your review what areas you consider yourself an expert in and where your expertise is limited. Avoid letting lack of methodological familiarity translate into unfair negative scoring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflect on and communicate personal biases / positionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect on and communicate your personal biases! Can you allude to your positionality as it shapes your perspective on the review?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider and disclose how your academic background, cultural perspective, and methodological preferences may shape your evaluation. Treat reviewing as an activity that, like research, has confounding factors to acknowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider academic school-of-thought assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: What does my academic school of thought consider, disregard, and remain unaware of? Is the paper I am reviewing making assumptions from the perspective of an academic school of thought or with bias?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of epistemological assumptions embedded in both the paper and your own perspective. Identify assumptions the authors make and whether those are appropriate or require justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalate substantive concerns to Area Chair (do not desk reject unilaterally)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you concerned about the content of a paper? ASK YOUR AC. Do not take it upon yourself to 'desk reject' a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you have major concerns (ethical, representational, etc.), raise them with the Area Chair / senior committee instead of unilaterally desk-rejecting. Use committee-only comments where appropriate to communicate sensitive concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect and report misrepresentation or biased portrayals of groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the paper unfairly misrepresent a group? Is there a group of people whose representation is unfactual or tainted with bias?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag instances where a paper misrepresents or unfairly characterizes groups. Provide evidence and suggest corrections; escalate serious issues to chairs if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report ethical concerns to chairs / Research Ethics Committee
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you concerned about the ethics of the work you are reviewing? If you have potential concerns on ethics, please contact your SCs and Papers chairs. Papers chairs will further escalate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should point out ethical concerns and discuss them with Senior Chairs / Papers Chairs and the Research Ethics Committee. The REC provides contextualization rather than direct accept/reject advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus review on magnitude of contributions and validity
rubrics_metrics.description: While the reviewers should point out any ethical concerns and discuss with SCs and Papers chairs (and the Research Ethics Committee), their reviews can focus on judging the magnitude of the contributions and the validity of the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Center your assessment on how significant the contribution is to the field and whether the work's claims are valid given the evidence and methods. Use other sections (ethics, accessibility, writing) to flag non-core issues but base overall recommendation on contribution and validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use community resources and specialized guides
rubrics_metrics.description: Many communities within SIGCHI have invaluable specialized guides (e.g. Mobile HCI, SIGCHI Accessibility Guide, Unofficial [crowdsourced] Guide to Reviewing for CHI, Transparency in Qualitative Research: Increasing Fairness in the CHI Review Process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult relevant SIGCHI community guides, accessibility resources, and methodological guidance tailored to the subfield when in doubt or when specialized expertise is required.
